property_summary: After any transferOwnership(newOwner) call initiated by the current owner, the contract's owner must equal the provided newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment breaks this because owner will not change to newOwner for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For any caller address X and any newOwner address Y, calling transferOwnership(Y) while msg.sender==X must only succeed in changing owner when X is the current owner; the reference C enforces that only the current owner can change owner, whereas the mutant allowing require(true) permits a non-owner to change owner for some inputs.

For all callers, calling owned() on the correct contract C does not change the owner state (owner remains the same); the mutant that removes the onlyOwner require allows non-owners to execute owned() and thereby can change owner for some caller inputs.
Calling owned() must never change the public owner variable when invoked by the current owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), violating this invariant for some callers.

For every caller who is the current owner, invoking owned() does not change the public owner variable; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so for some owner callers the owner will (improperly) change.

For every address a that is the current owner, calling C.owned() preserves the owner (owner remains equal to a); the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so when the owner calls owned() and msg.sender differs (via a contract caller that proxies the call), the owner can change — the test uses a contract proxy so msg.sender inside C is the proxy, proving the mutant breaks the invariant.

For every address a that is the current owner, a direct call to owned() from that same EOA preserves owner (owner stays equal to a); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() causes owner to change when the call originates from a proxy contract, so the invariant that an owner calling owned() does not change owner is broken for some inputs (a proxy address supplied by the fuzzer).

For every address a that is set as owner, calling owned() via a direct EOA call preserves owner (owner stays equal to a); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() breaks this when the owner calls through a forwarding contract (so owner becomes the forwarder address).

The reference contract enforces that only the current owner can change owner via transferOwnership (i.e., after any call to transferOwnership, the owner remains unchanged unless the caller was the previous owner); the mutant removes this restriction allowing non-owners to change owner.

For all callers and newOwner addresses, only the current owner can successfully change C.owner via transferOwnership; the mutant allows a non-owner caller to change owner, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every caller and target newOwner, only the current owner can make transferOwnership succeed (calls by non-owners do not change owner); the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows some non-owner callers to change owner, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner getter equals newOwner (the buggy mutant clears owner to address(0) and thus breaks this rule for some inputs).
